title: Compound Pendulum
short_intro: A compound pendulum is any rigid body mounted on a horizontal axis of rotation displaced from its center of mass, capable of oscillating freely under gravity. Its time period depends on its moment of inertia about the suspension axis and the distance from the center of mass to that axis.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definition, time period formula, relation with simple pendulum, and center of suspension/oscillation.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Kater's reversible pendulum, condition for maximum/minimum time period, equivalent simple pendulum length, and radius of gyration relations.

prerequisites: Simple harmonic motion and differential equation of angular oscillations
Moment of inertia and parallel axis theorem
Torque and angular acceleration dynamics for rigid bodies

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Restoring Torque
bullets: A rigid body of mass m is suspended about a horizontal frictionless axis O.
The distance from the center of mass G to the axis of suspension O is denoted by l or h.
The restoring torque for a small angular displacement theta is given by tau = -mg l sin(theta) approx -mgl theta.

concept_notes.heading: Equivalent Length of Simple Pendulum
bullets: The time period of a compound pendulum is identical to that of a simple pendulum of length L_eq.
The equivalent length is defined as L_eq = (I / m h), where I is the moment of inertia about the axis of suspension.
Using the parallel axis theorem, I = I_G + m h^2 = m k_G^2 + m h^2, where k_G is the radius of gyration about the center of mass.

concept_notes.heading: Interchangeability of Centers of Suspension and Oscillation
bullets: The center of oscillation is a point at distance L_eq from the axis of suspension along the line passing through the center of mass.
If the compound pendulum is inverted and suspended from the center of oscillation, its time period remains unchanged.
The distance between the center of suspension and the center of oscillation is always equal to the length of the equivalent simple pendulum.

concept_notes.heading: Conditions for Minimum Time Period
bullets: The time period depends on the distance h of the pivot from the center of mass.
Differentiating the time period expression with respect to h reveals that the time period is minimum when h equals the radius of gyration about the center of mass (h = k_G).
The graph of T versus h is symmetrical on both sides of the center of mass.

derivations.title: Time Period of a Compound Pendulum
derivations.conditions: Rigid body oscillating with small angular amplitude theta
steps: Write the equation of rotational motion: tau = I alpha, where alpha = d^2theta / dt^2.
Equate restoring torque to moment of inertia times angular acceleration: -m g h sin(theta) = I (d^2theta / dt^2).
For small theta, sin(theta) approx theta, yielding (d^2theta / dt^2) + (m g h / I) theta = 0.
Compare with standard SHM equation (d^2theta / dt^2) + omega^2 theta = 0 to get angular frequency omega = sqrt(m g h / I).
Substitute omega = 2 pi / T to obtain the time period T = 2 pi sqrt(I / m g h).

derivations.title: Equivalent Simple Pendulum Length and Radius of Gyration
steps: Express moment of inertia about pivot O using parallel axis theorem: I = I_G + m h^2 = m k_G^2 + m h^2, where k_G is radius of gyration about center of mass.
Substitute I into the time period formula: T = 2 pi sqrt((m k_G^2 + m h^2) / m g h).
Simplify the expression under the square root: T = 2 pi sqrt((k_G^2 + h^2) / (g h)).
Compare with simple pendulum formula T = 2 pi sqrt(L_eq / g) to define equivalent length.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of Time Period with Distance from Center of Mass
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of T (y-axis) versus h (x-axis) showing two symmetrical hyperbolic branches with a minimum time period at h = k_G.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: For any given time period other than T_min, there are four points of suspension (two on each side of COM) having the same time period.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in PGT to find the radius of gyration or acceleration due to gravity using intercept methods.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kater's Reversible Pendulum Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rigid bar with two fixed knife edges facing each other and two adjustable masses to equalize the time period when suspended from either knife edge.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: When the time periods about both knife edges are exactly equal, the distance between the knife edges is equal to the length of the equivalent simple pendulum, allowing precise measurement of g.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Theoretical questions regarding how Kater's pendulum eliminates errors due to unknown moment of inertia.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phase Portrait of Compound Pendulum Oscillation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Angular velocity (omega) versus angular position (theta) showing closed elliptical trajectories for small oscillations.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents conservative conservation of energy in phase space for the compound pendulum.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual PGT questions on phase space trajectories.

solved_numericals.question: A uniform rod of mass 2 kg and length 3 m is suspended about one of its ends. Find the time period of small oscillations. (Take g = 9.8 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Distance of center of mass from pivot h = L / 2 = 3 / 2 = 1.5 m.
Moment of inertia of a uniform rod about one end is I = (1/3) m L^2 = (1/3) * 2 * (3)^2 = 6 kg m^2.
Use time period formula T = 2 pi sqrt(I / (m g h)).

solved_numericals.question: A uniform circular disc of mass M and radius R is suspended about a horizontal pin passing through a point on its rim perpendicular to its plane. Calculate its equivalent length of simple pendulum.
solution_steps: Distance from the pivot (edge) to the center of mass is h = R.
Moment of inertia of a disc about its center of mass is I_G = (1/2) M R^2.
Using parallel axis theorem, moment of inertia about the edge is I = I_G + M h^2 = (1/2) M R^2 + M R^2 = (3/2) M R^2.
Equivalent length is L_eq = I / (M h) = ((3/2) M R^2) / (M R) = (3/2) R.

solved_numericals.question: Find the minimum possible time period of a uniform thin rod of length 2 m oscillating about a horizontal axis perpendicular to its length. (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Radius of gyration of a rod about its center of mass is given by k_G^2 = L^2 / 12.
The minimum time period occurs when h = k_G = 1 / sqrt(3) m.

assumptions_and_limitations: The angular amplitude is assumed to be very small (theta << 1 radian) so that sin(theta) approx theta is valid.
Air resistance and friction at the pivot are neglected for ideal harmonic motion.
The rigid body is assumed not to undergo any elastic deformation during oscillation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The time period of a compound pendulum depends only on its total mass.
common_misconceptions.correct: The time period depends on the ratio of the moment of inertia to the product of mass, gravity, and distance to COM (I / mh), making mass cancel out for uniform bodies.
common_misconceptions.why: Mass appears in both the restoring torque and inertial terms, hence cancels out.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The center of oscillation is always at the geometric lower end of the pendulum.
common_misconceptions.correct: The center of oscillation is at a distance L_eq from the pivot, which depends on the moment of inertia and may lie outside the physical body in certain configurations.
common_misconceptions.why: L_eq is determined strictly by dynamical parameters I and m h, not physical boundaries.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Minimum time period occurs when the pivot is at the center of mass.
common_misconceptions.correct: When the pivot is at the center of mass, h = 0 and the time period is infinite.
common_misconceptions.why: Zero restoring torque results in infinite time period.

quick_revision: Compound pendulum time period formula is T = 2 pi sqrt(I / mgh).
Equivalent simple pendulum length is L_eq = h + k_G^2 / h.
Minimum time period occurs when h = k_G.
Centers of suspension and oscillation are mutually interchangeable.
